name: Colin Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a cloud-only firm, about twenty-five of us, and our clients are freelancers, video makers and tiny app start-ups. I start with a coffee and a dashboard that shows which clients' bank feeds have synced overnight, then I prepare their year-end accounts and self-assessment tax returns. I use AI tools all day, to sort transactions, draft the notes to the accounts and summarise long client emails. What I love is building little shortcuts; what wears me out is that I'm still weak on the actual tax rules, and Hana, my reviewer, finds the same kind of mistake in my files every week.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly things like capital allowances, when someone buys a laptop or a camera and the tax treatment is different from the accounts. I get the process fast but the rules slowly. Sam, my boyfriend, fixes bikes for a living and says I'd be a terrible mechanic because I'd automate the wrench before learning which way it turns. He's not wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly, and I'd say so. I'd post something like the tools are still useful, they just aren't magic. At work I'd keep showing people my shortcuts, because they save real time even in the boring version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd probably be good for me. If nothing radical changes, I've got time to actually learn tax properly and become the person who's quick and also right. My pay's normal, I've got about five months saved, and there are other firms like mine if this one went wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book onto the firm's tax technical course in spring and do the self-study on Tuesday nights. I'd keep the savings growing by about a hundred and fifty a month. And I'd keep building tools, maybe a checklist bot for the capital allowances mistakes Hana keeps catching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Like a film trailer that was better than the film.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it'd be good for you. Is there anything in your life that worries you even if AI stays small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, a bit, it's about forty percent of my pay. And Sam's bike stall depends on good weather, so his winter months are thin. But we've done two winters like that and we're fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the people you show your shortcuts to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the tool's only as good as your checking. I learned that the hard way when an AI tool filed a client's train tickets under entertainment. I'd tell them to check what it does, every time, for the first month.

say: I'd post that AI tools are **still useful**, just not magic.
I'd keep sharing **shortcuts** at work, because they save real time anyway.
think: A plateau gives me **time to learn tax** properly and be quick and right.
With **five months saved** and similar firms nearby, my position feels solid.
do: Book the firm's **tax technical course** and study on Tuesday nights.
Grow savings by about **£150 a month**.
Build a **checklist bot** for the capital allowances mistakes Hana catches.
feel: **Calm** and a bit flat, like a trailer better than the film.
S0.quote: I learned that the hard way when an AI tool filed a client's train tickets under entertainment.
fieldNote: He's the firm's **AI enthusiast**, yet admits his tax knowledge lags his tool skills.
A plateau reads as **breathing room** to fix his weak spot.
Ordinary worries like **rent** and his partner's thin winters are present but feel handled.

steps.text: Take the firm's tax technical course this spring
Build a checklist bot for capital allowances errors
Keep preparing freelancer accounts with the same tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's make sure the gains get shared, shorter weeks, not fewer people. At work I'd volunteer to help roll out whatever we bring in. Online I'd argue with the people who think it's all hype and the people who think it's the apocalypse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the people who comes out okay, at least for a while. I'm already doing half the job with AI, so I'm the junior they keep to run the tools. But the firm won't hire new juniors, and that bothers me, because who trains up to be the next Hana?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager in the first month if I can lead our AI setup for new clients, and ask for a title and a small rise for it. I'd keep studying tax, because the tools still need someone who knows the rules. And I'd join the professional union, partly because I think someone in there should understand the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit guilty. Good for me, bad for the next lot coming through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be building the thing that stops my firm hiring someone like me two years ago. My friend Priya's finishing her accounting degree next summer, and I wouldn't know what to tell her. I'd probably tell her to learn the tools, which is a bit rich coming from someone who benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you push the union to ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A training levy, so firms that automate still have to fund trainee places somewhere. And a rule that time saved turns into shorter weeks at least partly. I don't think it'd win both, but it's worth asking.

say: I'd argue the gains should mean **shorter weeks**, not fewer people.
I'd volunteer to help **roll out** the firm's new tools.
think: I'm probably the junior they **keep to run** the tools, at least for a while.
The firm **won't hire juniors**, so nobody trains up to be the next reviewer.
do: Ask to **lead the AI setup** for new clients, with a title and small rise.
Keep studying **tax rules**, because the tools still need someone who knows them.
Join the **professional union** and push for a training levy.
feel: **Excited** and a bit **guilty** about the juniors coming next.
S1.quote: I'd be building the thing that stops my firm hiring someone like me two years ago.
fieldNote: He expects to **benefit** personally, as the junior who already works with the tools.
His worry is for **future trainees**, and his guilt feels genuine.
His union goal is a **training levy**, a practical progressive ask rather than a slogan.

steps.text: Ask to lead the AI setup for new clients
Keep studying tax rules alongside the tools
Join the union and push for a training levy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income now, not a debate about it. I'd be loud online, and at work I'd say out loud that this ends what we do here. I'd try to keep it practical, though: what do we owe the clients in the meantime?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the end of my job, and fast. Two years is enough time for AGI to do everything I do, including the tax rules I'm still bad at. The robots coming later doesn't help me, my whole job is a screen. Sam's work is hands-on, so he's got till about 2031, which is a weird thing to be grateful for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year helping small businesses set up AI for their own books, evenings and weekends, at maybe forty pounds an hour while that's still a thing people pay for. I'd push every penny over rent into savings, aiming to get from five months to a year. And I'd start learning bike repair with Sam on Saturdays, half as a joke, half not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but busy. I'd probably not sleep much, but at least I'd be doing things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said half as a joke. What's the half that isn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That hands-on work gets three more years, and Sam's stall could use a second pair of hands and someone who can do the books and the online booking. Hands-on bike repair isn't a career for me, it's a bridge. I'd rather build a bridge than stand on the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would ask if I should have been a doctor after all. I'd say even doctors would be in this. I'd tell my parents not to worry and then go home and worry.

say: I'd call for a **basic income** now, not another debate.
I'd say openly at work that this **ends what we do**, and ask what we owe clients.
think: Two years is enough for AGI to do **everything I do**, tax rules included.
Sam's **hands-on work** gets until about 2031, which I'm oddly grateful for.
do: Set up AI for **small businesses' books** at about £40 an hour, evenings and weekends.
Push savings from five months to **a year** of bills.
Learn **bike repair** with Sam on Saturdays as a bridge.
feel: **Scared** but busy, sleeping badly while doing things.
S2.quote: Hands-on bike repair isn't a career for me, it's a bridge. I'd rather build a bridge than stand on the edge.
fieldNote: Even the **most adaptive** person in the office expects his job to end within two years.
He uses the **three-year robot gap** practically, through his partner's bike stall.
He'd hide his fear from his **parents**, a gap between what he says and feels.

steps.text: Set up AI bookkeeping for small businesses at £40 an hour
Push savings from five months to a full year
Learn bike repair with Sam on Saturdays
Campaign online for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning we should use: basic income trials, training funds, all of it, and start now. At work I'd push us to tell clients the truth about what's coming. I'd probably start a newsletter about it, because I can't help myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to have a proper go at one more thing. I think I'd become the person at the firm who sets up AI for clients, then leave around 2029 to do that on my own. By 2031 that business probably dies too, but I'd have savings and I'd know a lot of small businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pass my tax exams by 2028 so I've got the qualification while it still counts. I'd launch a small AI-setup service on the side in 2027 and go full-time if it pays my rent. And I'd save half of anything I earn from it, aiming for a year's cushion by the time AGI lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can use. It feels like a race I might actually finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the business probably dies too. Why build it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the five years in between are real years. Somebody's going to be paid to help businesses through the five years before AGI. Better me than a big consultancy charging ten times more. And I'd learn what clients actually want from a person when the software's free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sam say about you leaving a steady job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say go for it, he's self-employed and thinks everyone should be. But he'd also want to know we're not touching the joint account. So I'd keep my own pot separate, with a hard stop if it drops under three months.

say: I'd push for **basic income trials** and training funds starting now.
I'd start a **newsletter** and urge the firm to tell clients the truth.
think: Five years lets me **have a go** at an AI setup business before 2031.
The business probably **dies too**, but I'd leave with savings and contacts.
do: Pass my **tax exams** by 2028 while the qualification still counts.
Launch a side **AI-setup service** in 2027, going full-time if it covers rent.
Save **half of side earnings**, aiming for a year's cushion.
feel: **Anxious** in a usable way, like a race I might finish.
S3.quote: Somebody's going to be paid to help businesses through the five years before AGI. Better me than a big consultancy charging ten times more.
fieldNote: He treats the five years as a **business window**, fully expecting it to close.
His risk-taking has a **hard stop**: never below three months saved.
His progressive views show in wanting to undercut **big consultancies** for small clients.

steps.text: Launch an AI-setup service for small businesses in 2027
Leave the firm around 2029 if the service covers rent
Save half of side earnings with a three-month floor
Push publicly for basic income trials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a decade to design the world after work, so let's actually design it. I'd get involved with a party or a campaign on basic income. At work I'd keep being the tools guy, but I'd say this is the time to build skills that aren't just screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine for most of it. I'd get qualified, good at tax, run the AI side at the firm, maybe become a manager by thirty-two. And with ten years I'd have time to slowly move into something hands-on or people-heavy before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, ask for the AI lead role, and invest a bit each month in an index fund, maybe two hundred. I'd join a basic income campaign properly, not just online. And around 2030 I'd start a part-time course in something hands-on, maybe electrics, so I'd have a trade by the time AGI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but curious more than scared. Ten years is a long time for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because everything with AI and robots still needs power run to it, and someone has to fit it until 2039 at least. Sam knows an electrician who's always behind on work. It also just sounds satisfying after years of screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana, honestly. She's forty-eight, brilliant at tax, and she hates change. Ten years is enough for me, but for my reviewer Hana it lands right before she'd want to slow down.

say: I'd say we have a decade to **design the world** after work.
I'd tell colleagues to build **skills beyond screens** while there's time.
think: I'd be **fine for most** of the decade, running the AI side at the firm.
Ten years gives time to move into **hands-on or people** work before 2036.
do: Qualify and ask for the **AI lead** role at the firm.
Invest about **£200 a month** in an index fund.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough for me, but for my reviewer Hana it lands right before she'd want to slow down.
fieldNote: A decade puts him firmly in **control**, and he reads it as opportunity.
His **electrics** idea follows the three-year robot gap and his partner's contacts.
He worries for an **older colleague** more than himself, matching his outlook.

steps.text: Ask for the AI lead role at the firm

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not for me so much, I'd scramble and manage, but because nobody would have time to build anything fair. What would help is a basic income that's ready before it hits, and cheap training in hands-on trades for people coming off screens. Also, honestly, some way to keep trainees learning, even if it's paid by the state.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want any of this. I use AI every day and I still don't want a world where nobody needs to learn how a tax return works. Being useful is part of being a person.

headlineQuote: I use AI every day and I still don't want a world where nobody needs to learn how a tax return works.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old junior** at a cloud-only firm serving freelancers and small start-ups.
He uses AI **all day** but is still weak on tax rules, and knows it.
In slower pictures he sees **opportunity**, from leading AI setup to a side business.
Fast AGI ends his job, and he leans on his partner's **bike repair** as a bridge.
His progressive views show in pushing for **basic income** and fair training for juniors.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because nobody would have time to build anything fair.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** ready in advance and cheap **hands-on training**.
A state-funded way to keep **trainees learning** the job.
